# Overview



Foundry is a comprehensive framework for protein design that provides unified tooling and infrastructure for using and training deep learning models across three critical domains: **design** (RFdiffusion3), **inverse folding** (ProteinMPNN and LigandMPNN), and **protein folding** (RosettaFold3). The framework enables end-to-end protein design pipelines by integrating these models through a common interface, all built atop [AtomWorks](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/atomworks) for biomolecular structure manipulation and processing.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L9)

## Architecture and Design Philosophy

Foundry follows a strict dependency hierarchy: `foundry` → `atomworks`, where **AtomWorks** handles structure I/O, preprocessing, and featurization, while **Foundry** provides model architectures, training infrastructure, and inference endpoints. This separation of concerns enables Foundry to serve as a unified platform for multiple independent protein design models, each packaged separately in the `models/` directory while sharing core infrastructure.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L36-L42)

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Models Layer"
        RFD3["RFdiffusion3<br/>Design"]
        RF3["RosettaFold3<br/>Folding"]
        MPNN["ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN<br/>Inverse Folding"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Foundry Core Layer"
        IE["Inference Engines"]
        TR["Training Harness<br/>FabricTrainer"]
        CM["Checkpoint Management"]
        HYDRA["Hydra Config System"]
        CB["Callbacks & Metrics"]
        DDP["Distributed Training<br/>DDP Support"]
    end
    
    subgraph "AtomWorks Layer"
        BIO["Biotite AtomArray"]
        FEAT["Featurization"]
        PREPROC["Preprocessing"]
        IO["Structure I/O"]
    end
    
    RFD3 --> IE
    RF3 --> IE
    MPNN --> IE
    
    IE --> TR
    IE --> CM
    TR --> HYDRA
    TR --> CB
    TR --> DDP
    
    TR --> FEAT
    IE --> PREPROC
    FEAT --> IO
    PREPROC --> BIO
    
    style Foundry fill:#e1f5ff
    style AtomWorks fill:#fff4e1
    style Models fill:#e1ffe1
```

The architecture is built around several core components:

- **BaseInferenceEngine**: Provides a unified interface for loading checkpoints and running inference across all models, separating expensive model setup from iterative inference execution
- **FabricTrainer**: A generic training harness built on PyTorch Lightning Fabric that supports gradient accumulation, mixed precision, distributed training, and native Exponential Moving Average (EMA) integration
- **Hydra Configuration System**: Manages complex model configurations with custom resolvers for dynamic parameter resolution
- **Checkpoint Management**: Centralized registry system for downloading and managing model weights with automatic path resolution

Sources: [base.py](src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L32-L66), [fabric.py](src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L1-L50), [resolvers.py](src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py#L1-L25)

## Supported Models

Foundry currently integrates three state-of-the-art protein design models, each addressing a different aspect of the protein design workflow:

| Model | Type | Primary Function | Key Features |
|-------|------|------------------|--------------|
| **RFdiffusion3 (RFD3)** | Design | Generate novel protein backbones under complex constraints | All-atom diffusion, supports nucleic acid binders, small molecule binders, enzymes, symmetry |
| **RosettaFold3 (RF3)** | Folding | Predict 3D structure from amino acid sequence | Competitive with AlphaFold-3, supports protein-DNA complexes, multiple checkpoint variants |
| **ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN** | Inverse Folding | Design sequences for fixed backbones | Lightweight, fast inference, supports ligand conditioning, soluble protein design |

![RFdiffusion3 Generation](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/blob/production/docs/_static/cover.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L20-L32), [all.ipynb](examples/all.ipynb#L10-L19)

### RFdiffusion3 (RFD3)

RFdiffusion3 is an all-atom generative diffusion model capable of designing protein structures under complex constraints including protein-protein, protein-DNA, protein-ligand, and enzymatic active site design. The model supports symmetric design and various conditioning modes for diverse design scenarios.

![Protein-DNA Complex](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/blob/production/docs/_static/prot_dna.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L20-L24), [rfd3/README.md](models/rfd3/README.md#L1-L14)

### RosettaFold3 (RF3)

RosettaFold3 is a structure prediction neural network that narrows the gap between closed-source AlphaFold-3 and open-source alternatives. It includes implicit chirality representations and atom-level geometric conditioning at train-time, improving performance on tasks such as prediction of chiral ligands and protein-DNA complexes. Multiple checkpoint variants are available for different use cases (latest, preprint, and benchmark).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L28-L32), [rf3/README.md](models/rf3/README.md#L1-L18)

### ProteinMPNN and LigandMPNN

These are lightweight inverse-folding models that design diverse sequences for backbones under constrained conditions. ProteinMPNN handles standard protein sequence design, while LigandMPNN extends this to include small molecules, ions, DNA/RNA, and other ligands. SolubleMPNN specializes in designing soluble analogues of membrane proteins. All models support legacy weight loading for backward compatibility.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L33-L35), [mpnn/README.md](models/mpnn/README.md#L1-L20)

## Key Features

### Unified Data Model

All models within Foundry rely on AtomWorks' Biotite `AtomArray` objects for both training and inference, providing a consistent data representation across the entire pipeline. This enables seamless interoperability between models without format conversion.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L9), [all.ipynb](examples/all.ipynb#L25-L27)

### Training Infrastructure

Foundry provides a comprehensive training harness with:

- **Distributed Training**: Native support for DDP (Distributed Data Parallel) across multiple nodes and GPUs
- **Precision Control**: Support for 64-bit, 32-bit, 16-mixed, and bfloat16-mixed precision training
- **EMA Integration**: Built-in Exponential Moving Average for model weight stabilization
- **Flexible Callbacks**: Modular callback system for metrics logging, health monitoring, and custom training events
- **Gradient Management**: Gradient accumulation, clipping, and NaN checking capabilities

Sources: [fabric.py](src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L1-L72)

### Configuration Management

The Hydra-based configuration system enables:

- **Dynamic Resolvers**: Custom resolvers for importing modules and resolving chain type information at runtime
- **Layered Configuration**: Base configs with model-specific overrides
- **CLI Overrides**: Powerful command-line override syntax for runtime parameter tuning

Sources: [resolvers.py](src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py#L1-L40)

### Checkpoint Management

A centralized CLI tool (`foundry install`) simplifies model weight management:

- **Automatic Registration**: Checkpoints are registered in a central registry for easy access
- **Hash Verification**: SHA256 verification ensures downloaded weights are uncorrupted
- **Progress Tracking**: Rich progress bars with download speed and time remaining
- **Flexible Installation**: Install individual models or all models at once

Sources: [download_checkpoints.py](src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L1-L50)

## Repository Structure

```
foundry/
├── models/              # Model-specific packages (independent)
│   ├── rfd3/           # RFdiffusion3 implementation
│   ├── rf3/            # RosettaFold3 implementation
│   └── mpnn/           # ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN implementation
├── src/
│   ├── foundry/        # Core shared infrastructure
│   │   ├── callbacks/              # Training callbacks
│   │   ├── inference_engines/      # Base inference engine
│   │   ├── metrics/                # Losses and metrics
│   │   ├── model/                  # Model layers
│   │   ├── trainers/               # FabricTrainer harness
│   │   ├── training/               # EMA, checkpoints, schedulers
│   │   ├── hydra/                  # Configuration resolvers
│   │   └── utils/                  # Utilities (DDP, datasets, etc.)
│   └── foundry_cli/   # CLI tools (checkpoint management)
├── examples/           # Jupyter notebooks (end-to-end pipelines)
└── tests/              # Test infrastructure
```

This structure enables a modular development workflow where core infrastructure (`src/foundry`) is developed once and reused across all model packages, while model-specific code remains isolated in the `models/` directory. Each model package has its own `pyproject.toml` and can be installed independently or in editable mode for development.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L44-L59), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L65-L85)

> [!TIP]
> The modular architecture means you can install only the models you need. Use `pip install rc-foundry[rfd3]` for just RFdiffusion3, or `pip install rc-foundry[all]` for all models.

## Installation and Quick Start

### Installation

Install Foundry with all models:

```bash
pip install rc-foundry[all]
```

Or install only specific models:

```bash
pip install rc-foundry[rfd3]  # Just RFdiffusion3
pip install rc-foundry[rf3]   # Just RosettaFold3
pip install rc-foundry[all]   # All models
```

### Download Checkpoints

Download model weights to a target directory:

```bash
# All models (approximately 6GB total)
foundry install all --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir

# Or specific models (recommended for beginners)
foundry install rfd3 ligandmpnn rf3 --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir
```

This sets the `FOUNDRY_CHECKPOINTS_DIR` environment variable, allowing models to be found automatically without specifying paths.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L12-L21), [download_checkpoints.py](src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L1-L50)

### End-to-End Example

The complete protein design pipeline demonstrates how the models work together:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Specifications<br/>Length, constraints] --> B[RFdiffusion3<br/>Generate backbone]
    B --> C[Generated Backbone<br/>AtomArray]
    C --> D[ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN<br/>Design sequence]
    D --> E[Designed Sequence<br/>+ Backbone]
    E --> F[RosettaFold3<br/>Validate structure]
    F --> G[Validated Design<br/>Confidence metrics]
    
    style B fill:#e1ffe1
    style D fill:#e1f5ff
    style F fill:#fff4e1
```

Sources: [all.ipynb](examples/all.ipynb#L23-L25)

# Quick Start



Foundry is a unified framework that provides tooling and infrastructure for using and training state-of-the-art models for protein design, including generative design (RFdiffusion3), inverse folding (ProteinMPNN and LigandMPNN), and structure prediction (RosettaFold3). All models within Foundry rely on AtomWorks for structure manipulation, preprocessing, and featurization during both training and inference. This Quick Start guide will walk you through installation, model setup, and basic usage for all supported models.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L6), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L24-L51)

## Architecture Overview

Foundry follows a strict dependency hierarchy where the core framework provides shared infrastructure that is extended by model-specific implementations. The architecture is designed with modularity in mind, allowing you to work with individual models or combine them into complete protein design pipelines.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["User Applications"] --> B["Foundry CLI"]
    A --> C["Model CLIs"]
    
    subgraph "Model Implementations"
        D["RFdiffusion3<br/>Generative Design"]
        E["RosettaFold3<br/>Structure Prediction"]
        F["ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN<br/>Inverse Folding"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Infrastructure"
        G["Inference Engines"]
        H["Training Harness"]
        I["Checkpoint Management"]
        J["Hydra Configuration"]
        K["Callbacks & Metrics"]
    end
    
    subgraph "External Dependencies"
        L["AtomWorks<br/>Structure I/O & Featurization"]
        M["PyTorch Lightning<br/>Training Framework"]
    end
    
    B --> G
    B --> I
    C --> D
    C --> E
    C --> F
    
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    
    D --> H
    E --> H
    F --> H
    
    G --> L
    H --> M
    J --> G
    K --> M
    
    style A fill:#e1f5ff
    style L fill:#ffe1e1
    style M fill:#ffe1e1
```

The architecture shows that Foundry provides a unified training and inference infrastructure that all models leverage. The core modules handle common concerns like configuration management, checkpoint loading, and distributed training, while model-specific code implements the unique architectures and inference logic for each model type.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L59-L64), [checkpoint_registry.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L33-L70)

## Installation

Foundry supports Python 3.12 or higher and can be installed with all model dependencies or with optional extras for specific models. The recommended installation method depends on your intended use case.

### Installation Options

| Installation Type | Command | Use Case |
|-------------------|---------|----------|
| **Complete** | `pip install rc-foundry[all]` | Full pipeline with all models (recommended for beginners) |
| **RFdiffusion3 only** | `pip install rc-foundry[rfd3]` | Generative protein design workflows |
| **RosettaFold3 only** | `pip install rc-foundry[rf3]` | Structure prediction tasks |
| **MPNN only** | `pip install rc-foundry[mpnn]` | Inverse folding and sequence design |

For development workflows, you can install Foundry and models in editable mode:

```bash
# Install foundry and all models in editable mode
uv pip install -e . -e ./models/rf3 -e ./models/rfd3 -e ./models/mpnn

# Or install only foundry (no models)
uv pip install -e .
```

The editable installation allows you to modify shared utilities in Foundry and see changes immediately, work on specific models without installing all models, and add new models as independent packages in the `models/` directory.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L8-L12), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L54-L66), [README.md](/README.md#L68-L81)

```
├── models/                          # Model-specific implementations

```

</details>

The `models/` directory contains all model-specific code, configurations, and documentation. The core Foundry infrastructure in `src/foundry/` provides shared functionality for training, inference, and utilities. The `examples/` directory contains Jupyter notebooks demonstrating usage patterns and complete workflows.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L59-L64), [get_repo_structure](/get_repo_structure), [checkpoint_registry.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L1-L20)

## Model Overview

Foundry supports three primary model families, each serving distinct protein design and analysis tasks.

![RFdiffusion3 cover](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/raw/production/docs/_static/cover.png)

| Model | Category | Primary Function | Key Capability |
|-------|----------|-------------------|----------------|
| **RFdiffusion3 (RFD3)** | Generative Design | Creates novel protein structures | Design under complex constraints (ligands, nucleic acids, symmetry) |
| **RosettaFold3 (RF3)** | Structure Prediction | Predicts 3D structures from sequence | Competitive with leading closed-source models, supports complexes |
| **ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN** | Inverse Folding | Designs sequences for fixed backbones | Handles ligands, DNA/RNA, and custom constraints |

![Protein-DNA complex](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/raw/production/docs/_static/prot_dna.png)

These models can be combined into complete design pipelines: RFD3 generates backbone structures, MPNN designs sequences, and RF3 validates or refines the designs.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L29-L52), [rfd3/README.md](/models/rfd3/README.md#L3-L7), [rf3/README.md](/models/rf3/README.md#L1-L14)

## Downloading Model Weights

All model checkpoints can be downloaded using the Foundry CLI, which provides a unified interface for checkpoint management with progress tracking and optional hash verification.

### Basic Download Commands

Download all models (complete pipeline):

```bash
foundry install all --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir
```

Download recommended beginner models:

```bash
foundry install rfd3 ligandmpnn rf3 --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir
```

Download individual models:

```bash
# RFdiffusion3 (generative design)
foundry install rfd3 --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir

# RosettaFold3 (structure prediction)
foundry install rf3 --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir

# ProteinMPNN (inverse folding)
foundry install proteinmpnn --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir

# LigandMPNN (ligand-aware inverse folding)
foundry install ligandmpnn --checkpoint-dir /path/to/ckpt/dir
```

> [!TIP]
> The checkpoint directory is optional and defaults to `~/.foundry/checkpoints` if not specified. After downloading, the CLI sets the `FOUNDRY_CHECKPOINTS_DIR` environment variable in your `.env` file, allowing you to run inference without supplying checkpoint paths in future runs.

### Available Checkpoints

| Model Name | Filename | Description | Size |
|------------|----------|-------------|------|
| `rfd3` | `rfd3_latest.ckpt` | Latest RFdiffusion3 checkpoint | ~3GB |
| `rf3` | `rf3_foundry_01_24_latest_remapped.ckpt` | Latest RF3 (data through Jan 2024) | ~2GB |
| `rf3_preprint_921` | `rf3_foundry_09_21_preprint_remapped.ckpt` | RF3 for benchmarking (data through Sep 2021) | ~2GB |
| `rf3_preprint_124` | `rf3_foundry_01_24_preprint_remapped.ckpt` | Original preprint RF3 | ~2GB |
| `proteinmpnn` | `proteinmpnn_v_48_020.pt` | ProteinMPNN weights (48 neighbors, σ=0.20) | ~500MB |
| `ligandmpnn` | `ligandmpnn_v_32_010_25.pt` | LigandMPNN weights (32 neighbors, σ=0.10) | ~500MB |
| `solublempnn` | `solublempnn_v_48_020.pt` | SolubleMPNN weights | ~500MB |

The download process includes automatic progress tracking and optional hash verification to ensure file integrity. Use the `--force` flag to overwrite existing checkpoints.

Sources: [download_checkpoints.py](/src/foundry_cli/download_checkpoints.py#L122-L150), [checkpoint_registry.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L33-L70)

## Running Your First Inference

Each model provides a command-line interface for inference. The examples below assume you have downloaded the checkpoints to your checkpoint directory.

### RFdiffusion3: Design a Protein Structure

RFdiffusion3 accepts design specifications in JSON format and generates novel protein structures satisfying your constraints.

```bash
rfd3 design out_dir=logs/inference_outs/demo/0 \
  inputs=models/rfd3/docs/demo.json \
  ckpt_path=null \
  skip_existing=False \
  dump_trajectories=True \
  align_trajectory_structures=True
```

Key parameters:
- `out_dir`: Output directory for results (auto-created)
- `inputs`: Path to JSON file specifying design constraints
- `ckpt_path`: Checkpoint path (use `null` to use default from `FOUNDRY_CHECKPOINTS_DIR`)
- `dump_trajectories`: Save intermediate diffusion steps (useful for visualization)
- `align_trajectory_structures`: Align trajectory structures for comparison

![Superimposed structures](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/raw/production/docs/_static/superimposed_80_residue_protein.png)

RFdiffusion3 supports diverse design scenarios including nucleic acid binders, small molecule binders, protein-protein interfaces, enzyme active sites, and symmetric assemblies.

Sources: [rfd3/README.md](/models/rfd3/README.md#L24-L38), [rfd3/README.md](/models/rfd3/README.md#L40-L48)

### RosettaFold3: Predict Structure from Sequence

RosettaFold3 predicts 3D structures from amino acid sequences and provides confidence metrics for quality assessment.

```bash
rf3 fold inputs='tests/data/5vht_from_json.json'
```

Specify a custom checkpoint:

```bash
rf3 fold inputs='tests/data/5vht_from_json.json' \
  ckpt_path='/path/to/rf3_checkpoint.ckpt'
```

Outputs include:
- `{input}_metrics.csv` - Overall confidence metrics (pTM, ptm_threshold, etc.)
- `{input}.score` - Granular confidence metrics per residue
- `{input}_model_{N}.cif.gz` - Compressed structure predictions for each diffusion seed

For high-confidence predictions, expect pTM values > 0.8 even without multiple sequence alignments.

Sources: [rf3/README.md](/models/rf3/README.md#L55-L78), [rf3/README.md](/models/rf3/README.md#L29-L50)

### ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN: Design Sequences

ProteinMPNN and LigandMPNN design sequences for fixed backbone structures, with LigandMPNN additionally supporting ligand-aware design.

```bash
# For protein-only design
mpnn inference model_type=protein_mpnn \
  backbone_path=/path/to/structure.pdb \
  out_dir=/path/to/output

# For ligand-aware design
mpnn inference model_type=ligand_mpnn \
  backbone_path=/path/to/complex.pdb \
  out_dir=/path/to/output
```

Important settings for legacy weights:
- `model_type`: Set to `"protein_mpnn"` or `"ligand_mpnn"`
- `is_legacy_weights`: Set to `True` for original model weights

> [!TIP]
> If you're benchmarking against original ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN models, use the old repositories until the Foundry API and public weights fully stabilize. The Foundry team is actively validating the re-implementation and welcomes feedback on discrepancies.

Sources: [mpnn/README.md](/models/mpnn/README.md#L34-L40), [mpnn/README.md](/models/mpnn/README.md#L63-L70), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L86-L88)

# End-to-End Design Pipeline Tutorial



This tutorial guides you through a complete *de novo* protein design workflow using Foundry's three core deep learning models: RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) for backbone generation, ProteinMPNN for sequence design, and RosettaFold3 (RF3) for structure validation. The pipeline demonstrates how to integrate these models to generate novel proteins with high designability.

![Protein Design Pipeline](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/blob/production/docs/_static/cover.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L30)

## Pipeline Overview

The end-to-end design pipeline follows a three-stage workflow that transforms from structural concepts to validated protein designs. Each model serves a specific purpose: RFD3 generates novel backbone conformations, MPNN designs amino acid sequences optimized for those backbones, and RF3 refolds the designed sequences to validate designability through structural prediction.

| Stage | Model | Purpose | Input | Output |
|-------|-------|---------|-------|--------|
| 1. **Backbone Generation** | RFD3 | Generate novel protein structures | Conditioning specifications | AtomArray structures |
| 2. **Sequence Design** | MPNN | Design sequences for backbones | Backbone AtomArrays | Designed sequences with structures |
| 3. **Structure Validation** | RF3 | Predict structure from sequence | Designed sequences | Predicted structures + confidence metrics |

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L9-L23), [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](/examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L21-L35)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Specifications] --> B[RFD3 Backbone Generation]
    B --> C[Generated Backbones<br/>AtomArray]
    C --> D[MPNN Sequence Design]
    D --> E[Designed Sequences<br/>with structures]
    E --> F[RF3 Structure Validation]
    F --> G[Refolded Structures<br/>+ Confidence Metrics]
    G --> H[RMSD Comparison]
    H --> I[Validated Design]
    
    style B fill:#e1f5fe
    style D fill:#fff3e0
    style F fill:#f3e5f5
```

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L17-L18), [base.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L32-L36)

## Prerequisites and Setup

Before running the pipeline, you must install Foundry with all model dependencies and download the required checkpoint files. The installation process requires approximately 6GB of storage for the model weights (3GB for RFD3, 3GB for RF3, and <100MB for MPNN).

```bash
# Install Foundry with all models
pip install 'rc-foundry[all]'

# Download model checkpoints
foundry install rfd3 ligandmpnn rf3
```

For Jupyter notebook users, register your foundry environment to enable model imports:
```bash
python -m ipykernel install --user --name=foundry --display-name "foundry"
```

> [!TIP]
> Set environment variables for optional mirror paths before importing: `CCD_MIRROR_PATH` for chemical component definitions and `PDB_MIRROR_PATH` for structure templates. This enables offline operation and faster data access.

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L40-L44), [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](/examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L14-L30)

## Step 1: Backbone Generation with RFD3

RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) is an all-atom generative model that produces novel protein structures through a diffusion process. The model accepts conditioning specifications that define design constraints, such as target length, fixed regions, symmetry requirements, or bound ligands.

### Configuration and Parameters

The `RFD3InferenceConfig` class provides comprehensive control over the generation process through several key parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `specification` | dict | `{}` | Conditioning specifications (length, contigs, symmetry) |
| `diffusion_batch_size` | int | 16 | Number of structures to generate per batch |
| `ckpt_path` | str/Path | `"rfd3"` | Checkpoint path or registered model name |
| `inference_sampler` | dict | `{}` | Diffusion sampling configuration |
| `cleanup_virtual_atoms` | bool | `True` | Remove virtual guidepost atoms from output |
| `dump_trajectories` | bool | `False` | Save intermediate diffusion steps |

Sources: [engine.py](/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L38-L77)

### Running Backbone Generation

Initialize the RFD3 inference engine with your specifications and run generation. The model outputs a dictionary mapping example IDs to lists of `RFD3Output` objects, each containing an `AtomArray` structure and associated metadata.

```python
from lightning.fabric import seed_everything
from rfd3.engine import RFD3InferenceConfig, RFD3InferenceEngine

# Set seed for reproducibility
seed_everything(0)

# Configure RFD3 inference
config = RFD3InferenceConfig(
    specification={
        'length': 80,  # Generate 80-residue proteins
    },
    diffusion_batch_size=2,  # Generate 2 structures per batch
)

# Initialize engine and run generation
model = RFD3InferenceEngine(**config)
outputs = model.run(
    inputs=None,      # None for unconditional generation
    out_dir=None,     # None to return in memory (no file output)
    n_batches=1,      # Generate 1 batch
)
```

Extract and visualize the generated backbone for downstream use:
```python
# Extract the first generated backbone
first_key = next(iter(outputs.keys()))
atom_array = outputs[first_key][0].atom_array

# Visualize the generated backbone
view(atom_array)
```

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L68-L107), [engine.py](/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L200-L264)

### Output Structure

Each `RFD3Output` contains the following components:
- **atom_array**: Full atomic structure as Biotite `AtomArray`
- **metadata**: Dictionary of generation metadata and conditioning information
- **example_id**: Unique identifier for the generated structure
- **denoised_trajectory_stack**: Optional stack of intermediate structures (if `dump_trajectories=True`)

The `RFD3Output` class provides a `dump()` method that saves structures to CIF format with optional JSON metadata files, facilitating external analysis and visualization in tools like PyMOL or ChimeraX.

Sources: [engine.py](/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L86-L130)

## Step 2: Sequence Design with MPNN

ProteinMPNN and LigandMPNN are inverse-folding models that design amino acid sequences optimized to fold into target backbone structures. MPNN uses a message-passing neural network to predict residue identities based on structural context, supporting both protein-only design and ligand-aware design scenarios.

### Model Selection and Configuration

MPNN provides two model types with different capabilities:

| Model Type | Description | Use Case |
|------------|-------------|----------|
| `protein_mpnn` | Original ProteinMPNN | Standard protein-only design |
| `ligand_mpnn` | Extended model with ligand support | Protein-ligand complex design |

The `MPNNInferenceEngine` accepts engine-level configuration (shared across all inputs) and per-input configuration (customized per structure):

```python
from mpnn.inference_engines.mpnn import MPNNInferenceEngine

# Configure MPNN inference engine
engine_config = {
    "model_type": "ligand_mpnn",  # or "protein_mpnn"
    "is_legacy_weights": True,    # Required for current weights
    "out_directory": None,        # Return results in memory
    "write_structures": False,
    "write_fasta": False,
}

# Configure per-input inference options
input_configs = [
    {
        "batch_size": 10,         # Generate 10 sequences per structure
        "remove_waters": True,    # Exclude water molecules
        "temperature": 0.1,       # Sampling temperature
    }
]

# Run sequence design
model = MPNNInferenceEngine(**engine_config)
mpnn_outputs = model.run(input_dicts=input_configs, atom_arrays=[atom_array])
```

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L112-L145), [mpnn.py](/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/inference_engines/mpnn.py#L40-L49)

### Key Inference Parameters

The MPNN inference pipeline supports extensive customization through per-input parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `batch_size` | int | 1 | Number of sequences to generate |
| `temperature` | float | 0.1 | Sampling temperature (lower = more confident) |
| `remove_waters` | bool | `None` | Exclude water molecules from context |
| `fixed_residues` | list | `None` | Residue indices to keep fixed |
| `designed_residues` | list | `None` | Residue indices to design (all if `None`) |
| `decode_type` | str | `"auto_regressive"` | Decoding strategy |
| `structure_noise` | float | 0.0 | Add noise to backbone coordinates |

Sources: [inference.py](/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/utils/inference.py#L36-L73)

### Extracting Designed Sequences

MPNN returns a list of `MPNNInferenceOutput` objects, each containing the designed sequence and corresponding structure. Convert residue names to one-letter codes for analysis:

```python
from biotite.structure import get_residue_starts
from biotite.sequence import ProteinSequence

# Extract and display designed sequences
for i, item in enumerate(mpnn_outputs):
    res_starts = get_residue_starts(item.atom_array)
    # Convert 3-letter codes to 1-letter
    seq_1letter = ''.join(
        ProteinSequence.convert_letter_3to1(res_name)
        for res_name in item.atom_array.res_name[res_starts]
    )
    print(f"Sequence {i+1}: {seq_1letter}")
```

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L147-L159)

> [!TIP]
> For design tasks requiring specific amino acid preferences, use the `bias` and `omit` parameters. `bias` assigns per-residue preferences (dictionary mapping positions to amino acid probabilities), while `omit` excludes specific residues from consideration globally.

Sources: [inference.py](/models/mpnn/src/mpnn/utils/inference.py#L63-L68)

## Step 3: Structure Validation with RF3

RosettaFold3 (RF3) predicts protein structures from amino acid sequences, validating that MPNN-designed sequences will adopt the intended backbone conformation. By comparing the RF3-predicted structure against the original RFD3 backbone, you can assess designability through RMSD and confidence metrics.

### RF3 Inference Configuration

The `RF3InferenceEngine` controls prediction quality through sampling and recycling parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `n_recycles` | int | 10 | Number of recycling iterations |
| `diffusion_batch_size` | int | 5 | Sequences processed per batch |
| `num_steps` | int | 50 | Diffusion steps for structure prediction |
| `template_noise_scale` | float | 1e-5 | Noise added to template structures |
| `early_stopping_plddt_threshold` | float | `None` | Stop recycling if pLDDT falls below threshold |

```python
from rf3.inference_engines.rf3 import RF3InferenceEngine
from rf3.utils.inference import InferenceInput

# Initialize RF3 inference engine
inference_engine = RF3InferenceEngine(ckpt_path='rf3', verbose=False)

# Create input from MPNN-designed structure
input_structure = InferenceInput.from_atom_array(atom_array, example_id="example_protein")
rf3_outputs = inference_engine.run(inputs=input_structure)
```

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L177-L195), [rf3.py](/models/rf3/src/rf3/inference_engines/rf3.py#L241-L256)

### Confidence Metrics

RF3 provides comprehensive confidence metrics for evaluating prediction quality:

| Metric | Description | Scale |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| `overall_plddt` | Per-residue confidence (average) | 0-1 (higher is better) |
| `overall_pae` | Predicted Aligned Error (average) | Å (lower is better) |
| `ptm` | Predicted TM-score | 0-1 (higher is better) |
| `iptm` | Interface pTM (multi-chain) | 0-1 (higher is better) |
| `ranking_score` | Combined quality metric | Higher is better |
| `has_clash` | Steric clash detected | Boolean |

The ranking score combines multiple metrics: `0.8 * ipTM + 0.2 * pTM - 100 * has_clash`, providing a single quality score for model selection.

```python
# Extract top-ranked prediction
rf3_output = rf3_outputs["example_protein"][0]

# Access summary confidences
summary = rf3_output.summary_confidences
print(f"Overall pLDDT: {summary['overall_plddt']:.3f}")
print(f"pTM: {summary['ptm']:.3f}")
print(f"Ranking score: {summary['ranking_score']:.3f}")
```

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L165-L182, #L197-L216), [rf3.py](/models/rf3/src/rf3/inference_engines/rf3.py#L79-L90, #L98-L146)

### Per-Atom Confidence Details

RF3 outputs granular confidence metrics for detailed analysis:

```python
conf = rf3_output.confidences

# Access per-atom/residue confidences
print(f"atom_plddts: {len(conf['atom_plddts'])} values")
print(f"PAE matrix: {len(conf['pae'])}x{len(conf['pae'][0])}")

# Preview first 10 atom pLDDTs
import numpy as np
print(f"First 10 atom pLDDTs: {np.round(conf['atom_plddts'][:10], 2).tolist()}")
```

The `atom_plddts` array provides per-atom confidence scores that can be mapped to B-factor columns for visualization in structural analysis tools.

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L218-L230)

## Validation and Design Assessment

The final validation step compares the RF3-predicted structure against the original RFD3-generated backbone using backbone RMSD. Low RMSD (< 2.0 Å) indicates the designed sequence is likely to fold into the intended conformation (high designability).

```python
from biotite.structure import rmsd, superimpose
from atomworks.constants import PROTEIN_BACKBONE_ATOM_NAMES
import numpy as np

# Get structures for comparison
aa_generated = atom_array              # Original RFD3 backbone
aa_refolded = rf3_output.atom_array    # RF3-predicted structure

# Filter to backbone atoms (N, CA, C, O)
bb_generated = aa_generated[np.isin(aa_generated.atom_name, PROTEIN_BACKBONE_ATOM_NAMES)]
bb_refolded = aa_refolded[np.isin(aa_refolded.atom_name, PROTEIN_BACKBONE_ATOM_NAMES)]

# Superimpose structures and calculate RMSD
bb_refolded_fitted, _ = superimpose(bb_generated, bb_refolded)
rmsd_value = rmsd(bb_generated, bb_refolded_fitted)

print(f"Backbone RMSD: {rmsd_value:.2f} Å")
print(f"Designability: {'Excellent' if rmsd_value < 1.0 else 'Good' if rmsd_value < 2.0 else 'Moderate'}")
```

### RMSD Interpretation Guide

| RMSD Range | Interpretation | Designability |
|------------|----------------|---------------|
| < 1.0 Å | Excellent agreement | High confidence |
| 1.0 - 2.0 Å | Good agreement | Moderate to high confidence |
| 2.0 - 3.0 Å | Moderate agreement | Consider redesign |
| > 3.0 Å | Poor agreement | Low confidence, redesign required |

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L232-L260)

### Exporting Results

Export structures to CIF format for external visualization and analysis:

```python
from atomworks.io.utils.io_utils import to_cif_file

# Export structures
to_cif_file(aa_generated, "generated.cif")
to_cif_file(aa_refolded, "refolded.cif")
```

![Superimposed Structures](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/blob/production/docs/_static/superimposed_80_residue_protein.png?raw=true)

Sources: [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L262-L273)

## Advanced Pipeline Configuration

### Batch Processing

Process multiple structures in parallel by adjusting batch sizes across all models:

```python
# RFD3: Generate multiple backbones
rfd3_config = RFD3InferenceConfig(
    specification={'length': 80},
    diffusion_batch_size=4,  # 4 backbones per batch
)

# MPNN: Design multiple sequences per backbone
mpnn_input_configs = [
    {"batch_size": 20} for _ in range(4)  # 20 sequences per backbone
]

# RF3: Predict multiple models per sequence
rf3_engine = RF3InferenceEngine(ckpt_path='rf3', diffusion_batch_size=5)
```

### Conditional Design

RFD3 supports complex conditioning through specification dictionaries:

```python
# Contig-based design with fixed regions
specification = {
    'contigmap': 'A20-30,B1-10,A31-40',  # Fixed regions
    'length': 80,
}

# Symmetry constraints
specification = {
    'symmetry': 'C3',  # Threefold symmetry
    'length': 120,
}

# Ligand-bound design
specification = {
    'ligand': 'path/to/ligand.cif',
    'hotspot_res': ['A10', 'A15', 'A20'],  # Interface residues
}
```

Sources: [engine.py](/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L425-L525)

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Issue | Symptoms | Solutions |
|-------|----------|-----------|
| **Out of Memory** | CUDA OOM errors during generation | Reduce `diffusion_batch_size` across all models; enable `low_memory_mode=True` in RFD3 |
| **Low Confidence** | pLDDT < 0.7, high PAE values | Increase RFD3 length specifications; add more fixed regions; redesign with higher MPNN `temperature` |
| **High RMSD** | RMSD > 3.0 Å after refolding | Generate more RFD3 backbones; use higher MPNN `batch_size`; check for design constraints conflicts |
| **Checkpoint Not Found** | `Invalid checkpoint` error | Run `foundry install <model>` or provide absolute path to checkpoint |
| **Slow Inference** | Long generation times | Increase batch sizes for GPU utilization; reduce `n_recycles` in RF3; disable `dump_trajectories` |

> [!TIP]
> For memory-constrained environments, use RFD3's `low_memory_mode=True` to enable efficient tokenization. This reduces peak memory usage at the cost of slightly longer initialization time.

Sources: [engine.py](/models/rfd3/src/rfd3/engine.py#L68-L70), [rf3.py](/models/rf3/src/rf3/inference_engines/rf3.py#L244-L246)

## Pipeline Flow Diagram

The complete end-to-end workflow integrates all three models with data flow transformations:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph RFD3["Step 1: Backbone Generation"]
        A1["Specification Config"] --> A2["RFD3InferenceConfig"]
        A2 --> A3["RFD3InferenceEngine.initialize"]
        A3 --> A4["run: Diffusion Process"]
        A4 --> A5["RFD3Output: AtomArray"]
    end
    
    subgraph MPNN["Step 2: Sequence Design"]
        B1["MPNNInferenceEngine Config"] --> B2["MPNNInferenceEngine"]
        B3["Engine-level params"] --> B2
        B4["Per-input params"] --> B5["run: Message Passing"]
        A5 --> B5
        B5 --> B6["MPNNInferenceOutput: Sequence"]
    end
    
    subgraph RF3["Step 3: Structure Validation"]
        C1["RF3InferenceEngine Config"] --> C2["RF3InferenceEngine"]
        B6 --> C3["InferenceInput.from_atom_array"]
        C3 --> C4["run: Recycling + Diffusion"]
        C4 --> C5["RF3Output: Structure + Confidences"]
    end
    
    subgraph Validation["Step 4: Design Assessment"]
        C5 --> D1["Backbone RMSD Calculation"]
        A5 --> D1
        D1 --> D2["Designability Score"]
        C5 --> D3["Confidence Metrics"]
    end
    
    D2 --> E["Validated Design"]
    D3 --> E
```

Sources: [base.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L125-L151), [all.ipynb](/examples/all.ipynb#L9-L23)

# Google Colab Quick Start



Get started with Foundry's protein design pipeline immediately using Google Colab—no local installation required. This interactive tutorial walks you through an end-to-end workflow combining three state-of-the-art deep learning models for protein design, all running in your browser with free GPU access.

![RFdiffusion3 Generation Trajectory](https://github.com/RosettaCommons/foundry/raw/production/docs/_static/cover.png)

This guide is perfect for developers who want to explore Foundry's capabilities without configuring a local environment or for those needing a quick proof-of-concept before committing to a full installation.

## Why Google Colab?

Google Colab provides an ideal platform for protein design experimentation:

| Advantage | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Free GPU Access** | T4 GPUs available without cost—essential for deep learning models |
| **Zero Configuration** | Pre-configured environment with Python 3.12+ |
| **Instant Setup** | Install and run in under 5 minutes |
| **Interactive Exploration** | Modify parameters and see results immediately |
| **No Resource Commitment** | Experiment without local disk space (~6GB for all models) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L15-L25)

## The End-to-End Pipeline

The Colab tutorial demonstrates a complete protein design workflow that mirrors professional workflows used at the Institute for Protein Design:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[GPU Runtime Setup] --> B[Installation<br/>rc-foundry[all]]
    B --> C[Download Weights<br/>~6GB total]
    C --> D[RFD3<br/>All-Atom Generation]
    D --> E[MPNN<br/>Sequence Design]
    E --> F[RF3<br/>Structure Validation]
    F --> G[RMSD Analysis]
    G --> H[Export Structures<br/>CIF format]
    
    style D fill:#e1f5ff

    style F fill:#e8f5e9
```

**Core Models:**

| Model | Role | Key Parameters | Output |
|-------|------|----------------|--------|
| **RFD3** (RFdiffusion3) | Backbone generation | `length`, `diffusion_batch_size`, `n_batches` | Novel protein structures as AtomArray |
| **MPNN** (ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN) | Sequence design | `batch_size`, `remove_waters`, `model_type` | Designed amino acid sequences |
| **RF3** (RosettaFold3) | Structure validation | Confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, pTM) | Predicted structure + confidence scores |

## Prerequisites and Setup

### 1. Enable GPU Runtime

Before running the notebook, ensure GPU acceleration is enabled:

1. Go to **Runtime → Change runtime type**
2. Select **T4 GPU** (or better—A100/V100 for faster runs)
3. Click **Save**

> [!TIP]
> GPU is mandatory. Running these models on CPU will be extremely slow and may time out for larger structures.

Sources: [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L5-L10)

### 2. Installation Process

The Colab notebook handles installation automatically:

```python
import os

# Set environment variables for AtomWorks mirrors
os.environ['CCD_MIRROR_PATH'] = ''
os.environ['PDB_MIRROR_PATH'] = ''

if not os.path.isfile("FOUNDRY_READY"):
    print("Installing rc-foundry...")
    
    # Uninstall torchvision first to avoid operator conflicts
    os.system("pip uninstall -y torchvision")
    
    # Install rc-foundry with all model dependencies
    os.system("pip install -q 'rc-foundry[all]'")
    
    # Mark as ready to skip re-installation
    os.system("touch FOUNDRY_READY")
    
    print("Done!")
else:
    print("rc-foundry already installed.")
```

**Key Points:**
- Installation occurs once per session (marked by `FOUNDRY_READY` file)
- `rc-foundry[all]` includes RFD3, MPNN, and RF3 packages
- Torchvision uninstalled to prevent version conflicts
- Installation typically takes 2-3 minutes on Colab

Sources: [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L13-L31)

### 3. Download Model Weights

```python
# Download model weights (~6GB total, skips already-downloaded models)
os.system("foundry install rfd3 ligandmpnn rf3")
```

**Download Breakdown:**

| Model | Size | Time (typical connection) |
|-------|------|---------------------------|
| RFD3 | ~3GB | 2-3 minutes |
| RF3 | ~3GB | 2-3 minutes |
| MPNN | <100MB | <30 seconds |
| **Total** | **~6GB** | **~5-7 minutes** |

> [!TIP]
> Weights download to Colab's temporary storage. They're cleared when your runtime disconnects, so you'll need to re-download for each new session.

Sources: [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L33-L36), [README.md](README.md#L16-L22)

## Step-by-Step Pipeline Walkthrough

### Step 1: All-Atom Generation with RFD3

RFD3 generates novel protein structures through diffusion, capable of designing under complex constraints:

```python
from lightning.fabric import seed_everything
from rfd3.engine import RFD3InferenceConfig, RFD3InferenceEngine

# Set seed for reproducibility
seed_everything(0)

# Configure RFD3 inference
config = RFD3InferenceConfig(
    specification={
        'length': 80,  # Generate 80-residue proteins
    },
    diffusion_batch_size=2,  # Generate 2 structures per batch
)

# Initialize engine and run generation
model = RFD3InferenceEngine(**config)
outputs = model.run(
    inputs=None,      # None for unconditional generation
    out_dir=None,     # None to return in memory (no file output)
    n_batches=1,      # Generate 1 batch
)
```

**Understanding the Output:**

```python
# Extract first generated structure for downstream use
first_key = next(iter(outputs.keys()))
atom_array = outputs[first_key][0].atom_array

# Visualize the generated structure
view(atom_array)
```

The `atom_array` is a Biotite `AtomArray` object—Foundry's universal structure representation that seamlessly flows through all models in the pipeline.

Sources: [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L61-L91), [rfd3/README.md](models/rfd3/README.md#L1-L10)

### Step 2: Sequence Design with MPNN

MPNN designs amino acid sequences that will fold into your target backbone:

```python
from mpnn.inference_engines.mpnn import MPNNInferenceEngine

# Configure MPNN inference engine
engine_config = {
    "model_type": "ligand_mpnn",  # or "protein_mpnn"
    "is_legacy_weights": True,    # Required for current weights
    "out_directory": None,        # Return results in memory
    "write_structures": False,
    "write_fasta": False,
}

# Configure per-input inference options
input_configs = [
    {
        "batch_size": 10,         # Generate 10 sequences per structure
        "remove_waters": True,
    }
]

# Run sequence design on the RFD3-generated backbone
model = MPNNInferenceEngine(**engine_config)
mpnn_outputs = model.run(input_dicts=input_configs, atom_arrays=[atom_array])
```

**Extracting Designed Sequences:**

```python
from biotite.structure import get_residue_starts
from biotite.sequence import ProteinSequence

# Extract and display the designed sequences
print(f"Generated {len(mpnn_outputs)} designed sequences:\n")

for i, item in enumerate(mpnn_outputs):
    res_starts = get_residue_starts(item.atom_array)
    # Convert 3-letter codes to 1-letter using Biotite
    seq_1letter = ''.join(
        ProteinSequence.convert_letter_3to1(res_name)
        for res_name in item.atom_array.res_name[res_starts]
    )
    print(f"Sequence {i+1}: {seq_1letter}")
```

**MPNN Variants:**

| Model | Use Case | Key Features |
|-------|----------|--------------|
| `protein_mpnn` | Protein-only design | Original ProteinMPNN |
| `ligand_mpnn` | Ligand-aware design | Handles small molecules, ions, DNA/RNA |
| `soluble_mpnn` | Soluble protein design | Optimized for solubility |

Sources: [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L119-L159), [mpnn/README.md](models/mpnn/README.md#L1-L30)

### Step 3: Structure Prediction with RF3

RF3 validates your design by predicting the structure from the designed sequence:

```python
from rf3.inference_engines.rf3 import RF3InferenceEngine
from rf3.utils.inference import InferenceInput

# Initialize RF3 inference engine
inference_engine = RF3InferenceEngine(ckpt_path='rf3', verbose=False)

# Create input from the MPNN-designed structure
input_structure = InferenceInput.from_atom_array(atom_array, example_id="example_protein")
rf3_outputs = inference_engine.run(inputs=input_structure)

# Extract the top-ranked prediction
rf3_output = rf3_outputs["example_protein"][0]
```

**Confidence Metrics:**

```python
summary = rf3_output.summary_confidences

print("=== Summary Confidences ===")
print(f"  Overall pLDDT:    {summary['overall_plddt']:.3f}")
print(f"  Overall PAE:      {summary['overall_pae']:.2f} A")
print(f"  pTM:              {summary['ptm']:.3f}")
print(f"  Ranking score:    {summary['ranking_score']:.3f}")
```

| Metric | Range | Interpretation |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| **pLDDT** | 0-1 | Per-residue confidence (>0.9 = high) |
| **PAE** | 0-∞ Å | Predicted Aligned Error (<2Å = good) |
| **pTM** | 0-1 | Predicted TM-score (>0.8 = high confidence) |

Sources: [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L193-L236), [rf3/README.md](models/rf3/README.md#L1-L20)

### Step 4: Validation and Export

The final validation step compares RF3's prediction against the original RFD3 backbone:

```python
from biotite.structure import rmsd, superimpose
from atomworks.constants import PROTEIN_BACKBONE_ATOM_NAMES

# Get structures for comparison
aa_generated = atom_array              # Original RFD3 backbone
aa_refolded = rf3_output.atom_array    # RF3-predicted structure

# Filter to backbone atoms (N, CA, C, O)
bb_generated = aa_generated[np.isin(aa_generated.atom_name, PROTEIN_BACKBONE_ATOM_NAMES)]
bb_refolded = aa_refolded[np.isin(aa_refolded.atom_name, PROTEIN_BACKBONE_ATOM_NAMES)]

# Superimpose structures and calculate RMSD
bb_refolded_fitted, _ = superimpose(bb_generated, bb_refolded)
rmsd_value = rmsd(bb_generated, bb_refolded_fitted)

print(f"Backbone RMSD: {rmsd_value:.2f} A")
```

**RMSD Interpretation:**

| RMSD (Å) | Designability | Action |
|----------|---------------|--------|
| <1.0 | Excellent | Proceed with confidence |
| 1.0-2.0 | Good | Acceptable for many applications |
| 2.0-3.0 | Moderate | Consider refinement or redesign |
| >3.0 | Poor | Redesign or adjust parameters |

**Export for Downstream Analysis:**

```python
from atomworks.io.utils.io_utils import to_cif_file

# Export structures to CIF format for visualization in PyMOL/ChimeraX
to_cif_file(aa_generated, "generated.cif")
to_cif_file(aa_refolded, "refolded.cif")
```

Sources: [ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb](examples/ipd_design_pipeline_collab.ipynb#L254-L290)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L8-L11)

## Common Issues and Troubleshooting

| Issue | Cause | Solution |
|-------|-------|----------|
| **Out of Memory** | GPU insufficient for batch size | Reduce `diffusion_batch_size` to 1 |
| **Slow Downloads** | Poor network connection | Download models individually instead of `all` |
| **Torchvision Conflicts** | Version incompatibility | Ensure torchvision uninstall runs before installation |
| **Runtime Disconnects** | Session timeout | Save checkpoints frequently; reduce model complexity |

# Architecture and Design Philosophy



Foundry embodies a modular, extensible architecture designed to support diverse biomolecular modeling tasks while maintaining clean separation of concerns. The framework provides shared infrastructure for training and inference across multiple protein design models, enabling developers to add new models with minimal code duplication.

## Foundational Architecture Principles

The architecture follows a strict dependency hierarchy: **foundry → atomworks**. This clear separation defines responsibility boundaries—atomworks handles all structure I/O, preprocessing, and featurization operations, while foundry provides model architectures, training harnesses, and inference endpoints. This design ensures that structural manipulation logic remains decoupled from modeling logic, allowing each layer to evolve independently.

The framework adopts a **package-per-model architecture** where each model (RF3, RFD3, MPNN) exists as an independent package within the `models/` directory. Each model package contains its own `pyproject.toml`, source code in `src/`, configuration files, and tests. This structure enables selective installation—users can install only the models they need, and developers can work on specific models without affecting others.

**Modularity through abstraction** manifests in two critical base classes. The `BaseInferenceEngine` separates expensive model initialization from inference execution, allowing multiple inference runs with minimal overhead. The `FabricTrainer` provides a reusable training harness built on PyTorch Lightning Fabric, implementing gradient accumulation, mixed precision training, distributed data parallelism, and native EMA support. Both classes employ the Template Method pattern, defining the skeleton of operations while allowing subclasses to customize specific steps.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L194), [README.md](/README.md#L58-L85), [base.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L32-L246), [fabric.py](/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L52-L924)

## Core Infrastructure Components

### Training Harness Architecture

The `FabricTrainer` class serves as the foundation for all model training, orchestrating the complete training lifecycle while providing extensibility points. The training harness follows a clear progression: initialization → model/optimizer/scheduler construction → Fabric setup → training loop → validation loop → checkpointing. This linear flow ensures predictable behavior while allowing customization at each stage through abstract methods and callbacks.

The harness implements **gradient accumulation** transparently, handling the complex logic of accumulating gradients across multiple batches before optimizer steps. Mixed precision training with bfloat16 or float16 reduces memory footprint while maintaining numerical stability. Distributed training support via DDP enables multi-node and multi-GPU scaling, with configurable NCCL timeouts and parameter discovery settings for production environments.

**Exponential Moving Average (EMA)** integration provides model weight smoothing without requiring users to implement complex tracking logic. The EMA module maintains a shadow model updated with a decay factor, automatically swapping between training and EMA weights during validation based on the training phase.

Sources: [fabric.py](/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L1-L8), [EMA.py](/src/foundry/training/EMA.py#L8-L68)

### Inference Engine Architecture

The `BaseInferenceEngine` establishes a **two-phase lifecycle**: initialization and execution. During initialization, the engine loads checkpoints, constructs the model pipeline using Hydra configuration, applies configuration overrides for transforms and samplers, and sets up distributed contexts if needed. During execution, the engine processes inputs through the pipeline, runs model inference, and returns structured outputs.

This separation optimizes resource usage—expensive operations like model loading happen once, while inference can run repeatedly without reinitialization. The engine supports flexible input formats including `AtomArray` objects, file paths, and dictionaries, automatically handling conversion through the pipeline system. Context manager support enables automatic cleanup with `with BaseInferenceEngine(...) as engine:` syntax.

**Configuration override mechanisms** provide granular control without modifying checkpoint configs. Users can override transform parameters, inference sampler settings, and trainer options through dotted key paths, enabling experimentation with different configurations while preserving original checkpoint configurations.

Sources: [base.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L32-L246), [checkpoint_registry.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/checkpoint_registry.py#L1-L71)

### Callback System

The callback architecture enables **composable lifecycle hooks** across training and inference. The `BaseCallback` class defines comprehensive hook points at fit boundaries, epoch boundaries, batch boundaries, optimizer steps, and checkpoint operations. This design separates cross-cutting concerns like logging, metrics computation, and health monitoring from core training logic.

Callbacks execute at deterministic points in the training lifecycle, with clear ordering semantics. The trainer invokes hooks sequentially at each defined point, passing trainer context to enable callbacks to inspect and modify training state. This enables use cases like early stopping, learning rate adjustment, metrics logging, and gradient monitoring without modifying trainer code.

Sources: [callback.py](/src/foundry/callbacks/callback.py#L9-L117)

## Configuration Management Philosophy

Foundry embraces **configuration-driven development** through deep Hydra integration. Configuration files define models, transforms, samplers, optimizers, and schedulers, with Hydra handling composition, inheritance, and overrides. This approach enables reproducible experiments without code changes—different configurations can represent entirely different training runs or inference scenarios.

**Custom Hydra resolvers** extend configuration capabilities with dynamic resolution at runtime. The `register_resolvers()` function registers resolvers for importing modules dynamically and converting chain type information to regex patterns. This enables configuration files to reference classes and functions by string paths, eliminating hard-coded imports in configuration files.

The resolver system exemplifies the framework's design philosophy: **flexibility through composability**. Rather than building complex configuration logic into the core framework, Foundry extends Hydra's capabilities with targeted custom resolvers that solve specific domain problems like dataset filtering by chain type.

Sources: [resolvers.py](/src/foundry/hydra/resolvers.py#L1-L78)

## Dependency and Package Organization

The monorepo structure follows **strict dependency boundaries** enforced through package layout. The `src/foundry/` directory contains shared infrastructure with no model-specific code. Each model in `models/<model>/src/` imports from foundry but maintains isolation from other models. This circular dependency prevention ensures clean upgrades and enables independent versioning of model packages.

**Hatch-based build system** packages multiple Python distributions from a single repository. The `packages` list in `pyproject.toml` defines which subpackages become installable distributions, while `force-include` directives ensure configuration files are packaged with models. This enables workflows like `uv pip install -e . -e ./models/rf3` for developers, while end users can install `rc-foundry[all]` or individual model packages.

The build system supports **dynamic versioning** via VCS integration, automatically deriving version numbers from git tags. This eliminates manual version management while ensuring reproducible builds across development and production environments.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L78-L111), [README.md](/README.md#L66-L85)

## Extensibility Patterns

Foundry enables extensibility through **abstract base classes with clear extension points**. New models extend `BaseInferenceEngine` and `FabricTrainer`, implementing abstract methods like `training_step()` and `validation_step()` while inheriting full training infrastructure. This eliminates boilerplate code for distributed training, checkpointing, and logging.

The **pipeline architecture** for data transformation provides a composable approach to preprocessing. Transforms are modular components that can be chained together, applied conditionally, and configured independently. Each model package defines its own transform library in a `transforms/` directory, reusing only the patterns from foundry rather than the implementations.

> [!TIP]
> When extending Foundry with new models, leverage the existing pipeline system by defining transforms as separate modules with clear input/output contracts. This maintains testability and enables transform reuse across different models even when the underlying architectures differ significantly.

Sources: [base.py](/src/foundry/inference_engines/base.py#L32-L246), [fabric.py](/src/foundry/trainers/fabric.py#L627-L654)

## System Architecture Overview

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Model Packages"
        RFD3["RFdiffusion3"]
        RF3["RosettaFold3"]
        MPNN["ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Foundry Core Infrastructure"
        direction TB
        InferenceEngines["BaseInferenceEngine"]
        Trainers["FabricTrainer"]
        Callbacks["BaseCallback System"]
        HydraConfig["Hydra + Custom Resolvers"]
        CheckpointRegistry["Checkpoint Management"]
        EMA["Exponential Moving Average"]
    end
    
    subgraph "External Dependencies"
        AtomWorks["AtomWorks<br/>Structure I/O & Featurization"]
        PyTorchLightning["PyTorch Lightning Fabric<br/>Distributed Training"]
    end
    
    RFD3 --> InferenceEngines
    RFD3 --> Trainers
    RFD3 --> Callbacks
    
    RF3 --> InferenceEngines
    RF3 --> Trainers
    RF3 --> Callbacks
    
    MPNN --> InferenceEngines
    MPNN --> Trainers
    MPNN --> Callbacks
    
    InferenceEngines --> CheckpointRegistry
    InferenceEngines --> HydraConfig
    
    Trainers --> EMA
    Trainers --> PyTorchLightning
    Trainers --> Callbacks
    Trainers --> HydraConfig
    
    InferenceEngines --> AtomWorks
    Trainers --> AtomWorks
```

This diagram illustrates the layered architecture where model packages depend only on foundry's abstract interfaces, never on each other. The foundry core provides shared implementations, while external dependencies like AtomWorks and PyTorch Lightning form the foundation.

## Key Design Trade-offs

**Simplicity vs. Flexibility**: Foundry prioritizes configuration-driven flexibility over code simplicity. Complex behaviors like distributed training, mixed precision, and EMA are handled by the framework rather than requiring users to implement them. This reduces the learning curve for common use cases while enabling power users to override defaults through configuration.

**Performance vs. Abstraction**: The callback system introduces minimal overhead while providing maximum extensibility. Hooks execute at well-defined points without complex conditionals, maintaining training loop performance while enabling cross-cutting concerns. The two-phase inference engine architecture optimizes for multiple inference runs after a single expensive initialization.

**Modularity vs. Integration**: Each model package maintains strict isolation, enabling independent development and testing. However, the shared foundry infrastructure ensures consistency in training behavior, checkpoint format, and logging across all models. This balance enables rapid prototyping of new models while preserving production-grade reliability.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L50), [common.py](/src/foundry/common.py#L8-L109)

## Architectural Principles Summary

| Principle | Implementation | Benefit |
|-----------|---------------|---------|
| **Separation of Concerns** | atomworks (structures) → foundry (models) | Independent evolution of structure handling and modeling logic |
| **Package-per-Model** | Isolated packages in `models/` | Selective installation, independent versioning, reduced coupling |
| **Abstract Base Classes** | `BaseInferenceEngine`, `FabricTrainer` | Consistent interfaces, reduced boilerplate, enforced patterns |
| **Configuration-Driven** | Hydra configs + custom resolvers | Reproducible experiments, no code changes for different runs |
| **Composable Callbacks** | `BaseCallback` lifecycle hooks | Cross-cutting concerns without modifying core logic |
| **Two-Phase Inference** | Initialize once, run multiple times | Optimal resource utilization for batch inference |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L58-L85), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L72)
